subject: physics
title: Transformers
key_idea: A transformer changes the size of an alternating p.d. An a.c. in the primary coil makes a changing field in the iron core, which induces a p.d. in the secondary coil. The turns ratio gives the p.d.s, and for 100% efficiency power out equals power in.

blocks.text: A transformer changes the size of an alternating potential difference. It has no moving parts.

items.meaning: The input coil, connected to the a.c. supply.
The output coil, where the new p.d. appears.
The core the two coils are wound on. Iron is used because it is easily magnetised.
Increases the p.d., so Vₛ > Vₚ.
Decreases the p.d., so Vₛ < Vₚ.

items.text: An alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing magnetic field.
The iron core carries this field, which changes direction, through the secondary coil.
The secondary coil cuts through the changing field, so an alternating p.d. is induced across its ends.
If the secondary is part of a circuit, an alternating current flows in it.

blocks.text: A transformer does not work with direct current. The current is steady, so the magnetic field does not change and no p.d. is induced.

items: An alternating current in the primary coil induces an alternating p.d. in the secondary coil.
The link between the coils is a changing magnetic field in the iron core.
A transformer only works with a.c.

blocks.text: The p.d.s across the coils depend on the number of turns on each coil.

blocks.label: Transformer turns ratio
where: Vₚ is the potential difference across the primary coil, in volts, V
Vₛ is the potential difference across the secondary coil, in volts, V
Nₚ is the number of turns on the primary coil
Nₛ is the number of turns on the secondary coil

items: More turns on the secondary coil than the primary gives a step-up transformer.
Fewer turns on the secondary coil gives a step-down transformer.

blocks.text: A primary coil of 1000 turns is connected to 230 V. The secondary coil has 50 turns. Find the secondary p.d.

diagram.alt: Calculate the secondary potential difference of a transformer from its turns and the primary potential difference.
diagram.question: A transformer has {Np} turns on its primary coil and {Ns} turns on its secondary coil. The potential difference across the primary coil is {Vp} V. Calculate the potential difference across the secondary coil.

items: Vₚ ÷ Vₛ = Nₚ ÷ Nₛ links the p.d.s to the turns.
More secondary turns means a higher secondary p.d.
Rearrange before substituting, and check the answer is higher or lower as expected.

sections.heading: Power, current and the National Grid

blocks.text: A transformer does not create energy. If it is 100% efficient, the power output equals the power input.

blocks.label: Transformer power
where: Vₛ × Iₛ is the power output from the secondary coil, in watts, W
Vₚ × Iₚ is the power input to the primary coil, in watts, W
Iₛ and Iₚ are the currents in the secondary and primary coils, in amperes, A

items: A step-up transformer raises the p.d., so the current in the secondary coil is lower.
A step-down transformer lowers the p.d., so the current in the secondary coil is higher.

blocks.text: A 100% efficient transformer has 230 V and 0.50 A in the primary coil. The secondary p.d. is 12 V.

Power is transmitted at high p.d. so that the current in the cables is small. A smaller current wastes less energy as heat. Transformers raise the p.d. at the power station and lower it again before it reaches homes.
Use the slider to see the p.d., current and power change.

diagram.alt: Change the turns on the coils and the primary current to see the secondary potential difference, the secondary current and the power of a transformer on 230 V mains.

items: Power out equals power in for a transformer that is 100% efficient.
Raising the p.d. lowers the current by the same factor.
High p.d. transmission means a small current and less wasted energy.

checks.q: Explain why a transformer does not work with a direct current.
checks.a: The direct current is steady, so the magnetic field in the core does not change. No potential difference is induced in the secondary coil.

checks.q: A transformer has 200 turns on the primary coil and 50 turns on the secondary coil. The primary p.d. is 120 V. Calculate the secondary p.d.
A transformer that is 100% efficient has 230 V and 0.50 A in the primary coil. The secondary p.d. is 11.5 V. Calculate the secondary current.

exam_phrases: a changing magnetic field around the primary coil
creates a magnetic field that changes direction in the core
the secondary coil cuts through the changing magnetic field
this induces an alternating potential difference across the secondary coil
iron, because it is easily magnetised (and demagnetised)
to vary the output potential difference

mistakes.wrong: The core is made of steel because it is magnetic.
mistakes.right: Steel is not accepted. The core is iron, because iron is easily magnetised (and demagnetised).

mistakes.wrong: The number of turns on the secondary coil can be changed to vary the power.
mistakes.right: Answers in terms of power are not accepted. Changing the turns varies the output potential difference, so the same generator suits different devices.
Convert kilovolts to volts first. 400 kV = 400 000 V, so Vₚ = 23 000 V. The answer is asked for in volts.

blocks.text: This content is Higher tier only and Physics only (Separate science) in this course. You do not need to know about laminations or eddy currents in the core.

worked_example.question:
A transformer has 345 turns on the primary coil and 6000 turns on the secondary coil.
The potential difference across the secondary coil is 400 kV.

Calculate the potential difference across the primary coil.
Give your answer in volts.
worked_example.tip: One mark for converting to volts, one for the substitution, one for the rearrangement and one for the answer.

exam_phrases: an alternating / changing current in the primary coil
magnetic field in the primary / secondary coil / core (due to current)
this magnetic field cuts / links the secondary coil
induces an alternating voltage across the secondary coil
substitution into Vₚ ÷ Vₛ = Nₚ ÷ Nₛ
input current × input voltage = output current × output voltage

mistakes.right: This inverts the ratio and earns one mark at most. Rearrange to Vₛ = Vₚ × Nₛ ÷ Nₚ = 230 × 18 ÷ 800 = 5.2 V.

mistakes.wrong: The changing magnetic field is caused by the voltage in the primary coil.
mistakes.right: References to voltage or potential difference are ignored. Say an alternating or changing current in the primary coil.
An upside-down rearrangement scores one mark for substitution only. Divide by 230: Iₚ = 19 × 2.37 ÷ 230 = 0.196 A.

worked_example.question:
A transformer has these values.
The number of turns on the primary coil, Nₚ = 800
The potential difference across the primary coil, Vₚ = 230 V
The number of turns on the secondary coil, Nₛ = 18

Calculate the potential difference across the secondary coil.
worked_example.tip: An answer that rounds to 10 000 scores one mark. Correct answer without working scores full marks.

exam_phrases: the current only flows in one direction
the magnetic field remains steady / does not change

mistakes.wrong: A transformer does not work with d.c. because no magnetic field is induced.
mistakes.right: 'Magnetic field not induced' is ignored. Say the current only flows in one direction, so the magnetic field stays steady and does not change.

mistakes.wrong: A transformer does not work with d.c. because electricity only flows one way.
mistakes.right: 'Electricity' is ignored. Use 'current', or voltage or p.d., and add that the magnetic field does not change.

worked_example.question:
A games console has a transformer built into its power cord.
The transformer decreases the potential difference of the mains supply from 230 V to 12.1 V.
The current in the primary coil of the transformer is 0.51 A.

Calculate the current in the secondary coil of the transformer.
Assume the transformer is 100% efficient.
worked_example.tip: Substitution and rearrangement can be in any order. Check the answer line first: 9.7 A gains all three marks.
